extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; economists, policymakers, and informed general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Expository chapter from a 19th-century political economy treatise arguing what capital is, how wages are generated, and how population/production relations (Malthusian theory) interact with wages. Presents principles about the functions and limits of capital and the origin of workers' subsistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wages originate from the produce of labor, not from capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages are that part of the produce of labor obtained by the laborer; they are created as labor is rendered and are not advanced by the employer from capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with the distinction between self-employed and wage-workers: a self-worker gets his wages in the things he produces as he produces them; a wage-worker creates his wages as he renders labor but receives them later in money. Except when wages are paid before work is done, the employer is not advancing capital to the laborer; rather the laborer during work is, in effect, advancing capital to the employer. Examples and thought experiments include the plowman, Robinson Crusoe, and circulating-exchange illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance of labor is drawn from contemporaneous production, not past hoarded capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The subsistence of laborers is, under normal conditions, supported by the current, contemporaneous production of the community rather than from previously hoarded wealth ('capital').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: the luxurious idler living off inherited power actually eats goods newly produced by others; a suspension of productive labor in a city would quickly cause starvation, showing people 'live from hand to mouth'; examples contrast past-saved stocks with everyday flows of production and exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of capital: wealth in the course of exchange used to procure more wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital consists of wealth used for the procurement of more wealth, i.e., wealth in the course of exchange; goods cease to be capital when they pass into the possession of those who will consume them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinction emphasized: articles of wealth are only capital so long as they remain in the possession of those who propose to exchange them for other commodities or productive services. When consumed for gratification they leave the category of capital regardless of whether consumption aids production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of capital — threefold (tools, reproductive nature, division of labor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital increases the power of labor to produce wealth by (1) enabling more effective application of labor (tools/machines), (2) permitting the utilization of nature's reproductive forces (seed, breeding), and (3) permitting the division of labor, increasing human efficiency and enabling specialization and broad exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: spade vs. hand, shovel for coal, sowing seed, factory machinery, storage/warehouses/transport for exchanges. Emphasizes that capital's role is to assist production, not to supply raw materials (nature supplies materials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital does not supply raw materials, wages, or maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital does not supply the materials which labor works up into wealth (nature supplies materials), nor does it advance wages or maintain laborers during production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restates that wages are the produce of labor, and consumption converted from goods held for exchange ceases to be capital when consumed. Footnote/example: paying for services from goods devoted to personal gratification is not payment from capital in the reproductive sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for consumption determines the direction of labor
rubrics_metrics.description: The demand for consumption determines the direction in which labor will be expended in production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed verbatim in the text and illustrated by exchange examples (jack-knives for wheat): by placing goods into exchange and demanding others, producers direct labor elsewhere to produce what they demand. The machinist producing an engine is, via demand, virtually producing the things he will consume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital may limit the form or productiveness of industry, but not the existence of industry itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital can limit the form of industry (e.g., factory operatives require factories) and the productiveness of industry by limiting the use of tools and the division of labor, but it does not strictly limit the exertion of labor or the possibility of industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: without a plow there'd be no plowmen, without sewing machines no machine sewing; yet in many contexts simpler tools are more efficient. The author argues scarcity of capital as sole limit is rare (war/devastation/new settlements aside), and often real limits are poor distribution of capital or social factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scarcity of capital is rarely the true cause of low productivity or poverty; distribution and social conditions matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Where industry is stunted, the true limitation is often misgovernment, insecurity of property, ignorance, or custom, not mere lack of capital; poor distribution or inability to employ capital profitably explains low use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses examples (Mexico, Tunis, new communities, indigenous peoples) where giving capital would not increase productivity unless accompanied by changes in social organization, education, and security. Notes rapid reproduction of capital after war and that a community tends to 'secrete' the necessary capital under healthy conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase in laborers does not necessarily reduce wages; wages derive from productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: If each laborer in performing labor creates the fund from which his wages are drawn, then wages cannot be diminished simply by increasing the number of laborers; other things equal, more laborers (increasing efficiency) should raise wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author adds the necessary proviso 'other things being equal' and flags that the productive powers of nature must also be considered; this sets up further inquiry into whether natural productivity diminishes with population increase (transition to Malthusian discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital is produced by labor; labor precedes capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital is itself the product of past labor and hence cannot be the antecedent cause of labor; there must be labor before there can be capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This underpins the critique of doctrines that treat capital as the source sustaining labor; used to reject theories that wages depend on a pre-existing stock of capital rather than on contemporaneous production and exchange.
